May there be auspiciousness! *Namaḥ* to the lotus feet of the venerable Aghoraśivācārya. *Dīkṣāvidhi-maṇipravālam*. Thursday, the 14th day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āni. (p.4a blank; p.4b, l.1) The preceptor (*ācārya*), who possesses the excellent qualities described in all the scriptures, having received a disciple while being endowed with such qualities, [bestows] the fruit of yoga and liberation. (l.2) The *darbha* garland.

Having constructed a pavilion according to the prescribed rites—adorned with great arches of *śamara* grass, banners, and the like, and further embellished with plantain and *kaṃgu* pillars—and having performed the daily and occasional *saṃdhyā* prayers, [he] should undergo an examination and purification without eating. ... pure...

In the space between Indra and Agni, having worshipped Śivasūrya in the *kumbha* as if for daily worship (*nityapūjā*), and having performed the *ācamana* and *sakalīkaraṇa* without the *uttāpana*, one should prepare the *sāmānyārghya*, place it in the left hand, and sprinkle the four doors starting from the east with "oṃ" at the eastern gate.

(Hāṃ) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the door of the Śāntikalā [residing] on the seat; (at the southeast) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the door of the Vidyākalā; (at the southwest) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the door of the Nivṛttikalā; (at the north) Oṃ hāṃ... (Prati)ṣṭhākalā door, salutation—having thus worshipped and circumambulated the pavilion, one should proceed clockwise from the east, placing these two deities at each door. (1) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nandin; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla; Oṃ hāṃ...

*Oṃ hāṃ Bhṛṅgiṇe namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ Vināyakāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ Vṛṣabhāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ Skandāya namaḥ*; *Devyai namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ Caṇḍāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped [these] in the pitcher (*kumbha*) preceded by meditation, and having first worshipped the door-keepers at the western gate... having entered within, [one should worship] on the pedestal: *Astrāya dvārapālāya namaḥ*.

Having circumambulated the sacrificial materials clockwise with the mantra "ye... and having worshipped Nirṛti (l. 3) preceded by meditation with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ vāstvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ," he performed the protection of the pavilion by means of the *astra-prākāra*, *kavaca*, and *aṅkuśa* mantras; then, in the station of Brahmā... [he became] the Lord.

To the south of Śiva, seated upon a seat such as a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) facing north, one should perform the *karanyāsa* as previously described. Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and invoked the Self (*ātman*) into the heart, one should subsequently place the forms of the seats (*āsanamūrti*) within the heart. Then, in accordance with the placement of the *kalās*, one should recite over the upper form (*ūrdhvamūrti*): "Oṃ Hom, obeisance to Īśāna, the omniscient, and to Śacī. [One should likewise recite] over the eastern form.

(1.7) Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of all beings, and to Kātyāyanī—thus at the southern face. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of all and the lord of the supreme Brahman, and to Brahmeṣṭā—thus at the northern face. Oṃ hūṃ, may Śiva be mine; obeisance to Marīcī—thus at the western face. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva and to Jvālinī.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *īśāna-kalās* upon the five faces—namely, the upper, eastern, southern, western, and northern—and having placed the *avyakta-kalā* upon the upper face with "Namaḥ," the *tattva-puruṣa-kalā* upon the eastern face with "Tatpuruṣāya Vidmahe Śāntyai Namaḥ," the *mahādeva-kalā* upon the southern face with "Oṃ Hāṃ Mahādevāya Dhīmahi Vidyāyai Namaḥ," and the *rudra-kalā* upon the northern face with "Oṃ Heṃ Tanno Rudraḥ Pratiṣṭhāyai Namaḥ."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the four *puruṣakalās* in the western face with "Oṃ haim praco-dayāt nivṛttyai namaḥ," and likewise in the upper, eastern, southern, and northern faces... thereafter, according to the method of placing the five *kalās* [of the *śakti*], one should perform the placement in the heart with "Oṃ huṃ aghorebhyas tamāyai namaḥ," and in the [western face] with "Oṃ huṃ aghorebhyo mohāyai namaḥ"; in the right arm with "Oṃ huṃ aghorarakṣāyai namaḥ."

Saying "Oṃ... Aghorebhyaḥ Nidrāyai Namaḥ," [he places it] on the left arm; saying "Oṃ Hūṃ Sarvatas Sarvatrutyai Namaḥ," on the navel; saying "Oṃ Hūṃ Sarvebhyo Māyāyai Namaḥ," on the belly; saying "Oṃ Hūṃ Namaste Rudrabhayāyai Namaḥ," on the head; and saying "Oṃ Hūṃ Rūpebhyo Jarāyai Namaḥ," on the chest—these are the Aghora-kalās.

Having performed nyāsa in these locations, then on the buttocks: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*, *rajāyai namaḥ*; on the liṅga: *oṃ hiṃ jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ*, *rakṣāyai namaḥ*; on the right thigh: *oṃ hīṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *ratyai namaḥ*; on the left thigh: *oṃ hiṃ kālāya namaḥ*, *pālyai namaḥ*; ...on the right knee: *oṃ hiṃ kalakāmāyai namaḥ*.

Saying "Oṃ hiṃ vikaraṇāya namaḥ saṃyamanyai namaḥ," [he places it] on the left thigh; saying "Oṃ... lakṣmyai namaḥ," on the right shank; saying "Oṃ hiṃ vikaraṇāya namaḥ buddhyai namaḥ," on the left shank; saying "Oṃ hiṃ pālakyai namaḥ," on the left calf; saying "Oṃ hiṃ pramathanāya namaḥ dhātryai namaḥ," on the hip region; and saying "Oṃ hiṃ sarvabhūtadamanāya namaḥ... [on the other hip].

Saying "Oṃ Ṛṇyai namaḥ," [he places it] on the right side; saying "Oṃ Hiṃ Manomohinyai namaḥ" on the left side; and saying "Unmanāya namaḥ" and "Bhayāyai namaḥ," these are the Vāmadeva-kalās. Having performed nyāsa in these locations, he then says "Oṃ Haṃ Sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi Siddhyai namaḥ" on the right foot, and "Oṃ Haṃ Bhave Lakṣmyai... and "Haṃ Sadyo... on the left foot.
Saying "Oṃ namo ṛddhyai namaḥ," [he places it] on the right hand; saying "Oṃ haṃ bhave dvityai namaḥ," on the left hand; and saying "Oṃ haṃ bhave lakṣmyai namaḥ," on...

Saying "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Medhā in Anādhibhava," one should perform nyāsa on the head; saying "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Kānti, please favor me," on the right arm; saying "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Svadhā in Bhava," on the left arm; and saying "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Udbhava and obeisance to Dhṛti," [one should perform nyāsa]. Having thus performed nyāsa for all seven Sadyojāta-kalās in these locations, and likewise having performed nyāsa for the thirty-eight kalās with their respective mudrās, [one should contemplate] the Vidyā-deha.

Having performed the Nyāsa of the eyes, the root-mantra, the heart and other limbs, as well as the protection (rakṣā) and veiling (avakuṇṭhana), one should display the Mahāmudrā while reciting the root-mantra. Thereafter, having performed the inner sacrifice (antaryāga), the fire-oblation (homa), and meditation (dhyāna), one should perform the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi) preceded by the three claps of the hands (tālatraya), and [offer] rice and sesame seeds...

He states that [the ritual] extends up to the Śiva-tattva by means of rice, *darbha* grass, flowers, milk, and water; he states the special *arghya* water for the purposes of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) by means of the items beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*); he states that it extends up to the Vidyā-tattva by means of the *nirodhārghya*; he states that it extends up to the Ātman-tattva by means of the sprinkling of the bound soul (*paśu-prokṣa*) and the installation of the Lord (*pati*) along with the mantras using the special *arghya* water.

Having sprinkled his own head... (l. 7), he should sprinkle the sacrificial materials such as flowers with the Astra-mantra while holding Darbha grass, perform an *abhyukṣaṇa* with the Kavaca-mantra, consecrate them with [the respective] mantras, and perform an *avakuṇṭhana* with the Kavaca-mantra. Having applied a tilaka of sandalwood paste on his forehead and performed the purification of the mantra for self-worship (*ātmabhūjā*), he should thereafter [proceed] toward himself... (p. 7a, l. 1).

Having performed the Nyāsa of Śivana on the head using the Āsana-mūrti-mantras, he performs the Nyāsa of the five Kalās according to the path of emanation (sṛṣṭimārga). Then: From the *brahmarandhra* to the forehead: *oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*. From the forehead to the heart: *oṃ hyaiṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. From the heart to the navel: *oṃ huṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*. From the navel to the knees: *oṃ hvīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*. From the knees to the feet: [oṃ hvoṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ].

(l.4) Vāk: *Oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*. Having thus meditated upon the partless Śiva as pervading the entire aggregate of Śiva-mantras, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in these locations, and having performed the assignment of the limbs beginning with the heart (*hṛdayādyaṅganyāsa*), the protection (*rakṣā*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the great mudrās (*mahāmudrā*), and having adorned himself with perfumes and flowers, he shall perform the "Śiva-hand" (*śivahasta*).

Having smeared the *gandha* with the thumb of the left hand upon the right hand, and having worshipped the *āsana-mūrtis*, he worships Īśāna and the others, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger. Having performed the *vidyā-deha-netra-nyāsa* and invoked Śiva, he assigns the limbs (*aṅgas*) starting from the little finger, performs the *paramīkaraṇa*, and enters his own *brahmarandhra* in the head. By that mass of light, [he destroys] the darkness both external and internal.

Having dispelled the obstructions and visualized all the *dikpālas* (guardians of the directions) as consisting of light, he then consecrated with mantras the *jñānakaṭaka*—a ring sixteen *aṅgulas* in height made from thirty-eight *darbha* grasses—which he took in his hand and placed within the maṇḍala as a witness for the rites, [visualizing] Śivanāga fire... [visualizing] Śiva himself as the presiding deity of the *mātṛkā*... [visualizing] the primordial source (*yirāṇ*)... (Note: The ellipses indicate portions of the text where the original manuscript is damaged or illegible.)

After the *pāvilu* [purification], one who is performing the *pañcagavyasnāna* (the ritual bath with the five products of the cow)—in accordance with the procedure—should prepare a mandala on the ground to the south of the western door in the presence of the deity. Having drawn nine compartments within it, he should place [the mantra] in the central compartment: *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ*. [Oṃ hāṃ] *supratiṣṭhapātrāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the vessel and consecrated the *paśu* within it once by means of the Īśāna-mantra, [one places it] in the eastern compartment... "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the compartment of the essence of Sadāśiva. Having thus worshipped the compartment and [worshipped] the vessel with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of supreme peace," one consecrates the *tattva* within it twice by means of the [Tattva-mantra], and [places it] in the southern compartment with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the compartment of the essence of Vidyā."

Having worshipped the eastern compartment with "Oṃ hāṃ tejovatpātrāya namaḥ" and the vessel with the same, one should consecrate the *kṛta* [food] therein with the Aghora mantra and prepare it in three ways. In the northern compartment, [worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ ... koṣṭhāya namaḥ. Having worshipped the vessel with "Oṃ hāṃ ratnodakapātrāya namaḥ," one should place *gojala* therein with the Vāmadeva mantra.

Having consecrated the *prakāra* with mantras, one should worship the *koṣṭha* in the western section with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *koṣṭha* of the principle of Time (*kālatattva-koṣṭha*)," and the vessel within that *koṣṭha* with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel consisting of nectar (*amṛtātmaka-pātra*). Having worshipped the vessel there, one should consecrate cow-dung with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) by means of the *Satyājāta* [mantra], and worship the *koṣṭha* in the northeastern section with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *koṣṭha* of the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva-koṣṭha*)," and the vessel within it with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of the unmanifest (*avyakta-pātra*)."

Having thus worshipped the vessel, one should sprinkle kuśa-water into it while consecrating it eight hundred times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) according to the prescribed method. Then, having gathered the cow-dung and other materials in the center by way of the sequence of dissolution (*saṃhāra-krama*), and subsequently having gathered the kuśa-water with the root mantra, and then having consecrated the kuśas with the *saṃhitā-mantra*, one should perform the protection (*rakṣā*), the binding (*ava-kuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). Regarding the matter of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), he says: having consecrated [it] eight hundred times with the root mantra.

Subsequently, since materials such as ghee, sandalwood, white mustard seed powder (*bhasma*), flowers, *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and *dūrvā* grass serve as the substances for the oblation (*homadravya*), it is not merely ghee alone [that constitutes the oblation]. (p. 8b, l. 1) ...

Having consecrated the materials in eighteen ways with the Astra-mantra, and having consecrated each of the specific substances—beginning with the *nīrājana-paṭa* and the *pāśa-sūtra*—with the Mūla-mantra once each; thereafter, standing in the north of the Nirṛti direction facing north, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *arghya*, using the Astra-mantra. Then, having performed the sixteen purificatory rites (*ṣoḍaśa-saṃskāra*), beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with *catuṣpadāna*, within the sacrificial hall...

For the purpose of removing all obstacles (*aśeṣavighna*) and for the sake of special purification (*viśeṣaśuddhi*), one should [place] all substances... not by rubbing with the *astra-mantra*, nor on a cold cloth, nor with *darbha* grass, nor with a *śamī* leaf, but as a seat upon a pedestal (*vardhanikā*) in the northeast (*īśāna*) corner. Afterwards, having worshipped the Lord of the Site (*vāstvadhipati*) in the northwest (*nirṛti*) corner, [one should worship] Mahālakṣmī in the space between Skanda and Vāyu with:
"Oṃ hāṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ."
Having meditated upon and invoked the dark-complexioned Sumukhī at the door— who rains down floods of flowers and jewels— the wise one should worship her and remember her in the form of the pavilion.
Having thus purified [the site] and worshipped Mahālakṣmī, he then [worshipped] Śiva and Śakti within the golden water-vessels that had been constructed, as well as within the earthen water-vessels.

Having surrounded [the vessel] with a book so that the worshipper may perform the ritual, and having filled it with water, [one should place] gold (*svarṇa*), the nine gems (*navaratna*), mercury (*rasa*), camphor and other fragrant substances (*sugandha*)... [with] oil, anointed with sandalwood (*candana*), and [the fruits of] *śūtapallava*, *aśvatthapallava*, and *ṭāḍimīpallava*—among these, one together with... [the fruit of] *tenga* (p. 9a, l. 1)... [the fruit of] *mātuḷaṅga* being placed therein.

How does one perceive the Śivakumbha, which is blood-red in color and surrounded by white cloth? Having placed that [vessel] within the [central] area... having offered those seven grains of rice in the northeast corner as a lotus and placed it upon that, one should worship the Śalāsana and the Ṣaḍutthāsana within that kumbha. Therein, beginning with the Āsana-mūrti, one should worship Śiva together with his limbs and accompanied by the enclosures (āvaraṇas), facing toward the Meru.

Having worshipped Tāṇī—who is situated to the south of the [main] deity and is endowed with the previously mentioned [attributes]—to the south of the *kumbha*, facing west at a distance of one *muṣṭi* (fist-length), and having worshipped here the *Pāśupatāstra* together with its limbs beginning from the *āsana-mūrti*, then, inside the pavilion, in the center for the sake of pacification (*śānti*) and for Mahākāla... [one should offer]: *Oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*; in the southeast (*agni-dik*), *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*.

Between Vidyā and Vighneśvara: Oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ. In the direction of Nirṛti: Oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ. Between Nivṛtti and Skanda: Oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ. Between Vighneśvara and Mahālakṣmī, in the direction of Vāyu: Oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ. Between Pratiṣṭhā and Caṇḍa: Oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ. In the direction of Īśāna: Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ.

Between Īśāna and Nandin: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Between Nirṛti and [Vāyu]: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having thus performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) for these [deities] along with their weapons, and having visualized them as remaining within the pavilion, one should worship them with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, saying: "O Cakra, by your command, for the sake of pacifying obstacles in your own direction, you must remain vigilant until the conclusion of the sacrifice, by the order of Śiva."

Having made a petition to the guardians of the quarters (dikpālakas) regarding the *śivāstrayai*, and thereafter taking up the *vardhanī* and standing over it, [one should place] the *kumbha* before the stream of water (*jaladhārā*)... beginning with "Namaḥ sarvātma-kāya," one should perform the meditation on the fourfold weapon (*astracatuṣka-mahādhyāna*), utter the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and circumambulate to the right; as before, one should recite the introductory verse (*purastuti*) for the *kumbha*. ...

Having placed the *vardhanī* behind him, he establishes Śiva upon the *sthirāsana*. He performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ādhāraśakti*, the *āsanamūrti-vidyā*, the body, and the eye, according to the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*). Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthāpana*), and other rites, as well as the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) as before, he then worships the *pāśupatāstra* while seated upon the *siṃhāsana* and facing westward. "Oṃ, *huṃ phaṭ* to the seat of the weapon; *namaḥ* to the form of the weapon.
[He meditates on it] resembling ten million suns and possessing the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Three-eyed, with nine... four-faced and four-armed;
his appearance is blazing and bewildering, with flaming eyebrows, fangs, and upward-pointing hair;
he holds a spear, a mallet, a trident, and a club, and bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

Having meditated in this manner, [one] worships the form... offers the eye [mantra], and performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) with: *oṃ ślīṃ bhaḥ suṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Then, having performed the stabilization (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm confinement (*sannirodhana*), [one places the mantras] in their respective locations: *oṃ hāṃ astrahṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, *oṃ ślīṃ astraśirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, *oṃ bhaṃ astraśikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, *oṃ huṃ astrakavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.

Having performed the *aṅganyāsa*, protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) with the mantra: "Astranetre hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; oṃ phaṭ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and having worshipped with all the services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) along with the *layāṅga* and *bhogāṅga* offerings, [one should worship] with "oṃ hlāṃ ... śivaśaktibhyāṃ namaḥ. If one desires worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), one should touch the *liṅgamudrā* at the jar with the thumb and the wick (*vartanī*).
If one desires liberation, one should touch the pitcher with the clenched fist and the vardhanī with the thumb. [Then recite:
"O Umā, obeisance to you who possess the form of the yoni, who assume all forms, and who are Śaṅkara."

Having thus offered praise and prostrated, he performed the *sthaṇḍila-pūjā* (worship on the sacrificial ground). Then, having petitioned: "O Mountain, since you are indeed the Lord of this [place] by virtue of your established nature, and since your form is eternal and free from weapons, please accept this weapon," he placed the sword in his right hand. Afterwards, with the *mūla-mantra*, [he recited it] one hundred and eight times...

Having recited the *Daśāṃśa-pāśupatāstra* mantra therein and offered it, he requested the protection of the sacrifice, saying: "The shadow of that [sacrifice] which has been set in motion by me, the sacrificer, must be protected by you; therefore, let there be its completion... Having thus entreated for the protection of the sacrifice, he gave the *nirōdārghya* with the *aghora* mantra and placed the *nirōdārghya-pātra* steadily in that spot.

Having worshipped Vināyaka between Vāyu and the Goddess, [I pray: "May that effort which was initiated by us later in the sacrifice of Sureśa for the sake of bestowing grace upon you proceed without obstacle in your presence."

Having thus petitioned Vināyaka, and having worshipped the seven Gurus between Caṇḍeśvara and Īśāna, thereafter—whether in the Brahma-... river, or in that Jayamaṇḍala which is the Kaurilathai-maṇḍala, or within a maṇḍala drawn with sandalwood paste—the Paramakāruṇika Śiva, who is the Lord of the sacrifice (adhvarapati), resides. [One should worship Him] as the āsana-mūrti, vidyā-deha, netra, śānti, atīta, and so forth; thus he describes the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), beginning with the placement of the kalās (kalānyāsa) and the invocation (āvāhana). ...

Having worshipped [the deity] according to the measure of the *liṅga*, one should thereafter worship the limbs of the body (*bhogāṅga*) through the five coverings (*pañcāvaraṇa*). In the first covering, one should worship the limbs of Brahmā as before, having performed the bathing (*snāna*) and worshipping them in their respective locations. In the second covering, one should worship Ananta and the other Vidyeśvaras, according to the verse:
"The Vidyeśvaras have four faces and ten arms like Hara;
all of them—Aṇḍa, Indu, and Kaula—reside upon lotuses and bear various weapons."
They hold a sword, a shield, a bow, and arrows, as well as a water-pot and a rosary;
they are endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and hold a trident and a lotus in their hands.

[The colors] are gold, fire, a cluster of moons, snow, and white gems, respectively. (p. 11a, l. 1) Thus, preceded by meditation, one should worship up to Īśāna as follows: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ sūkṣmāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ śivottamāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ ekanetrāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ ekarudrāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ trimūrtaye namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ śikhaṇḍine namaḥ*. Having worshipped in this manner, one should worship Gaṇeśvara, beginning with Nandin, in the third enclosure at the eastern direction.
One should meditate thus: Ratna-nandi has four arms, one face, three teeth, and matted hair;
he holds a rosary and a trident, and is endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Having meditated in this manner, [one should recite] "Oṃ hāṃ nandinē namaḥ" in the southeast.
Three-eyed, with yellow and black limbs, his beard and hair matted,
Mahākāla bears in his hands a skull-bowl, a sword, a shield, and a trident.

Having meditated in this manner, [recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ mahākālāya namaḥ* (l. 6) ... in the direction... (*Oṃ hāṃ*) *bhṛṅgiṇe namaḥ nir māṃsavikrahe*. Bhṛṅgin is white, holding a staff and a rosary; he is eternally three-eyed, crested, and intent upon the vision of the gods. Having meditated thus, [recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ bhṛṅgiṇe namaḥ ye* (l.
7) in the northwest direction (*nirṛti-dik*). Trimetra is short in stature, elephant-faced, and pot-bellied.
He carries a noose, a goad, his own tooth, and a ripe mango fruit.

With his trunk and left hand, the leader of obstacles (Vighnanāyaka) has a red body. Having performed meditation in this manner, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ. On the eastern side [of Varuṇa] is Vṛṣa, who has the form of a bull, possesses three eyes, and whose mind is solely intent upon Rudra.
And he is the very embodiment of the Dharma, as pure as a flawless crystal.
Having meditated in this manner, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ vṛṣabhāya namaḥ ye.

To the northeast: Skanda, four-armed, with the appearance of a youth, possessing a golden luster, holding a spear and a cock in his hands, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Skanda.
In the northern direction: The goddess is seated upon a lion, yellow in color, and holds a trident in her two pairs of hands.
She wears a crown adorned with a casket and is embellished with pearls and other ornaments.
Having meditated in this manner, one should say: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to the Goddess. Then, in the Īśāna direction:
Caṇḍeśvara has four arms and four faces, possesses three eyes, and holds a water-pot, a rosary, and a battle-axe.
One should meditate upon him who is enriched by a girdle of great serpents, whose bracelets are [like] that very [girdle],
who has the luster of a fresh cloud, and who is the regulator of the pledges (*samaya*) and other rules.
Having meditated in this manner, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Caṇḍeśvara.
Among these, Gajānana is seated upon a rat;
Skanda has a peacock as his vehicle; and Vṛṣabha stands alone.

Having thus meditated upon and worshipped [the deities], one should worship the guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra in the four directions. In the directions starting from the East and ending with the Northeast, one should place:
Airāvata, mounted on an elephant, golden-hued, and wearing a crown. airāvataṃ gajārūḍhaṃ svarṇavarṇaṃ kirīṭinam ।
One should visualize [Indra] with a thousand eyes, holding a discus and a thunderbolt in his hand. Thus is the meditation. Oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ.
[He is] bearing the seven-flamed fire, as well as a rosary and a water-pot.

[Visualize him] red, surrounded by garlands of flames, holding a spear in his hand, and seated upon a goat. Having meditated thus, [recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*. [Then visualize] Kṛtānta, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in his hand, and terrifying.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Southern Quarter, who is black, holds the noose of Time, and [is seated upon] a corpse; his eyes are red, and he has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
Thus having meditated, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Yama.
[He is] red-eyed, mounted upon a corpse, and possesses the brilliance of the petal of a blue lotus.
Thus meditating upon the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who holds a sword in his hand and drinks the flood of blood—
*Oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*—
[one should worship] the black one holding a serpent-noose, whose body possesses the luster of a mass of jewels.
One should meditate upon the deity of Varuṇa, white as the moon, mounted on a sea-monster (makara). Having performed meditation in this manner, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ.
[Then one should meditate on him] possessing a lush green luster and bearing a fluttering banner.
And [one should meditate upon] Vāyu, the life-force of all beings, seated upon a deer. Having thus performed meditation, one should say: "Oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ.
[Then one should meditate upon] Kubera, seated on a man, proud, and of short stature.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Northern Quarter, who has a golden luster and holds a mace in his hand. Thus is the meditation. [Recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ*.
[Then meditate upon] Īśāna, mounted upon a bull, holding a trident and a serpent.
Having meditated thus upon the one with the face of a young moon, the moon-crested, three-eyed Lord, recite:
*Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*.
Then, in the northeast [direction], [visualize] the yellow, stout, four-armed Brahmā with four faces.
Visualizing him thus, bearing a swan-vehicle and holding a staff, [rosary], and a water-pot—
reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ Brahmaṇe Namaḥ"—
one should meditate upon Ananta in the northwest, lotus-eyed and endowed with a thousand hoods.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] who resembles a flash of lightning, who has the form of a jar (*kumbha*), and who has joined his palms in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*);

one should worship with "Oṃ Hāṃ Viṣṇave Namaḥ. Then, for the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*) and the inner enclosure (*anāvaraṇa*), one should worship the ten thousand [deities] according to the following sequence from the east to the northeast:
"Vajra shall be Puruṣa, gross, firm, and of a harsh form."
One should worship the powerful Vajramūrdhan, who is radiant, in the southeast direction.

Having meditated in this manner, [one recites]: *Oṃ hāṃ vajrāya namaḥ*. Śakti, in the form of a woman, red in color, bearing a trident upon her head and stationed within a triangle—her I take refuge in.

Having meditated in this manner, [recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ śaktaye namaḥ. Then, having meditated thus: "The staff (daṇḍa) is also a person (puruṣa), black in color with red eyes," [recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ daṇḍāya namaḥ."
Visualizing a sword and a dark-complexioned man with eyes enraged at the body, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ.
[Then visualize] a seven-hooded serpent with a tail, accompanied by seven men.

Having meditated in this manner, [one recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ pāśāya namaḥ. Then, having meditated thus: "The banner (dhvaja), however, is the Puruṣa; it is yellow, with a face turned away and mighty arms," one recites: "Oṃ hāṃ dhvajāya namaḥ."
Having performed meditation in this manner—[visualizing] the daughter [of the mountain] with her very plump hips, [holding] a mace and a lotus—recite:
*Oṃ Hāṃ Gadāyai Namaḥ*.
The divine person [is] the trident, whose body is dark blue like the sky.
Thus, having performed meditation (l. 7), [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ triśūlāya namaḥ.
Then, having performed meditation upon Īśāna thus: "The divine Puruṣa is in the lotus, white-limbed and with auspicious eyes," [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ" (l. 8)... [in that place].

I worship the one with a hundred-spoked wheel, marked by a wheel on his feet, whose head is shaped like a man, who has a dark-blue body, and who holds the Mukunda weapon, located in the south-western corner.

Having meditated in this manner and worshipped with "Oṃ... Namaḥ," one should, in the fifth enclosure, contemplate all [the deities] with hands joined in *añjali* and heads marked by *vajras*, starting from the east. Having thus contemplated and worshipped the ten... [as before], all the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the others stand facing the deity.

Having addressed all the deities beginning with Ananta as those who are gazing upon the Lord, and having petitioned them, saying, "I shall worship Maṇḍaleśvara with the five coverings (pañcāvaraṇa), perform japa, present the offering (nivedita), and conduct the fire sacrifice (homa)," [he proceeds] toward the direction of Yama, Nirṛti...

To the north, having left this space, at a distance of one cubit from the [central] mark, there should be a pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one aṅgula in depth, joined with an upper layer of earth (upari-mṛd), and possessing a circumference of three aṅgulas; it should be joined with three layers of earth (mṛd-ala) starting from the upper layer of earth, reaching a height and width of three aṅgulas, and occupying half of that [space] within the pit. Therein, three...
O you who possess a mass of hair reaching the height of half a finger as a measure, rising seven fingers long; O you whose form resembles a royal leaf; O you who have shaken the crest of the cloud...

(1.7) Being joined with the navel which resides within the *māpūraka*, situated in the center like a lotus flower together with a *vajra* and a *padma*, and being thus unattainable—[he] shall take the *kuṇḍa* held in the right hand along with the *sāmānyārghya*, and having reached it while keeping that supreme navel foremost, he shall place the *arghya* and other items on the left side, and the vessels for the *homa* on the right side. (p. 13b, l. 1) He shall place them in the birth-order.

Thereafter, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra with the ring finger and thumb, having looked at it with the four [fingers], having sprinkled it with the root mantras, having performed the striking (*tāḍana*) with *darbha* grass using the *astra-mantra* ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, having performed the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the *vaśat* ending of the *antaka-mantra*, one should perform the piercing (*vedhana*) with the *astra-mantra*, the extraction (*uddhāraṇa*), the filling (*pūraṇa*), the harmonizing (*samīkaraṇa*), the seating (*sēcana*), and the pounding (*kuṭṭana*).

Having performed the sweeping (*saṃmārjana*) and the smearing (*samālepana*), and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits (*kalās*) beginning with Śāntyatītā in the south-east, south-west, north-west, and north-east directions, one should encircle [the pit] with a well-strung cord while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavacamantreṇa*). Then, having worshipped the pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ kalāmaya-kuṇḍāya namaḥ*.

Having cut [the darbha grass] with three darbhas pointing eastward and one darbha pointing northward, perform the *vajrīkaraṇa* of these three darbhas along with their roots using the *astra-mantra*. Having performed the *catuṣpadā-nyāsa* with two darbhas pointed toward the northeast using the *astra-mantra*, place them within the *kuṇḍa* and [arrange] many darbhas in the four directions using those darbhas.
Having performed the *akṣapādana* (the ritual of foot-washing) with the armor-mantra (*kavacamantreṇa*), one should place the *viṣṭara* in the form of a seat, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara.

Then, the wise practitioner should duly invoke the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātaram*) into that [seat], meditating upon her as dark-complexioned, in her menses, and adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments.
[Visualizing her] with a serene countenance, like a lotus, and possessing three eyes resembling petals—(l. 2)—...
reciting "Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ" while thus meditating, [recite] "Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ" for Vāgīśvara, and "Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvari-vāgīśvarābhyāṃ namaḥ."

Having worshipped these with *kanda-puṣpa* flowers, one should bring fire from the house of a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire (*agnihotra*)—whether it be from a wooden vessel, an earthen vessel, or a pure vessel—from the eastern direction. Having placed it in the southeast, the southwest, the northeast, and the northwest, one should consolidate all that fire into a single fire... [omitted] ...and having purified it with the *astra-mantra*, one should place it in the northwest corner.

Having performed purification through observation and other means, [recite] *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*. Then, having drawn [the fire] inside by means of the *pūraka* breath and the *saṃhāramudrā*, while performing *kumbhaka*, [visualize it] together with the fire situated at the *bindusthāna*. [Recite] *oṃ hāṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ*.

Thus, having joined the *reca* breath with the *utpatti-mudrā* and the fire residing within the vessel (*pātrasthamāna*), and having worshipped it for a mere moment (*saṃhitāmātra*)... [l. 8] ...by means of that, having performed the protection and enclosure (*rakṣāvakūṇḍana*), having rendered it nectarine (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* ending with *vauṣaṭ*, and having meditated upon the *śiva-bīja* as a threefold radiance circling clockwise above the *kuṇḍa*, one should contemplate the Lords of Speech (*vāgīśvaras*) as having their heads reaching toward the directions starting from Īśāna and being joined together.

In the *nāḍī* of Vāgīśvarī, [one should perform] the *ādāna* (taking up) of Vāgīśvara-nāla; having established this according to the traditional practice, one should place fire into the *kuṇḍa* for oneself by means of the *mūla-mantra*. Having visualized that the *parivarta* has been cast into the *śakti*, one should offer *arghyodaka* (water of honor) into the heart for the sake of purification (*sauca-śamana*), and [protect] with this *kavaca* of the *nāḍī*...

Having worshipped Garbhāgnī with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ huṃ garbhāgnaye namaḥ* while blazing with the Astra-mantra, and having placed Darbha grass consecrated by the Astra-mantra into his hand for the protection of the embryo (*garbharakṣārtham*), he should worship [the child] with Satyājāta for the occasion of the delivery of the embryo (*garbhādāna-nimittam*) and offer curd with the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having performed the *puṃsavana* rite, he should worship with Vāmadeva and offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with the *śiras* mantra; for the occasion of the *sīmantonnayana*, he should worship with Aghora and offer three oblations with the *śikhā* mantra; for the occasion of [birth], he should worship with Tatpuruṣa and offer three oblations with the *kavaca* mantra; and at the time of birth, for the purpose of removing the impurities of the womb (*garbhamala*), he should perform a bath using the *astra* mantra...

Having offered the *bindu* and kindled the fire with *darbha* grass and other materials, he takes the bundle of *darbha* blades upon which the Goddess’s hand has rested and visualizes it as being composed of a mass of gold.

Having worshipped [the deity] for the sake of concluding the *sūtakānta* (end of birth/impurity), one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with drops of *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*. Then, having performed the sprinkling (*tāḍana*) with *darbha* grass using the *astra-mantra*, and having performed the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the *vaṣaṭ*-mantra, for the purpose of protecting the fire, one should place *darbha* grass in the northeast, north, east, west, and south directions—northward and eastward. ...the *darbha* grass...

Having caused [the materials] to fly up with the Astra-mantra and having placed the *paridhi* enclosures, one should perform a homa with five kinds of fuel-sticks (*pañcasamit*) smeared with ghee at the feet and on the head—both for the purpose of removing the saliva from the mouth of the Fire-god and for the nourishment of the Fire—with the Astra-mantra. Afterwards, within the *paridhi* enclosures, in the eastern direction: *Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; and in the western direction: *Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ" in the southern direction and "Oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ" in the northern direction, [he should worship] upon the *viṣṭara* seats in the directions starting from the east and ending at the northeast: "Oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ," and "Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ."

Having worshipped in the northeast with "Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ" (l. 8), and having worshipped in the [western] direction with "Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ," and having offered the arghya and dispelled obstacles, he requests Śivāgni, saying, "Please protect this Agniśiśu" (p. 15b, l. 1). Thereafter, in order to perform the saṃskāra of the sruk and sruva, he places the sruk facing upward and the sruva facing downward, and [prepares] the darbha grasses (l. 2).

Having secured them, sprinkled them with the Astra-mantra, and performed the sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa) and the encircling (avakuṇṭhana) with the Kavaca-mantra, one should touch the tips of those [blades of] Kāśa grass with the tips of Darbha grass using the Hṛdaya-mantra while over the fire. Then, moving the fire to the right, one should again touch them with their nine Darbha blades, including the middle one.

Having touched the base of the surrounding [deities] together with the base of the *darbha* grass, and having returned and touched the surrounding [deities] again with the *darbha* grass, one should enter the central space and recite: "Oṃ hūṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ | Oṃ hūṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ |" Then: "Oṃ hiṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ | Oṃ hīṃ vidyātattvādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ |" And: "Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ |"

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahman, the supreme lord of the self-principle," one should perform nyāsa in the *sruc* with "Oṃ hāṃ... and in the *sruva* with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva. Having meditated upon them as Śakti and Śiva, one should take both [ladles] with the *mūla-mantra* and, circling them around the neck, place them upon *darbha* grass to one's right. One who worships them with the *hṛdaya-mantra* thereafter proceeds to purify the self (*ātma-śuddhi*) as follows: [with] *paśu-vinnam* (sesame)...

Having poured [the ghee] into the vessel and performed purification through inspection and other rites, one should meditate upon oneself as having the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahmā. Taking the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one places it around the fire and performs the oblation (*homa*) with a blade of *darbha* grass, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā. Then follows the installation (*sthāpana*).

Meditating on [the deity] in the form of *rūpa*, place it in the northeast direction and perform the *homa* with the tip of *kuśa* grass, reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave svāhā. ... Meditating on [the deity] in its subtle (*sūkṣma*) essential nature (*svarūpa*), place it at the navel and perform the *homa* with the tip of *kuśa* grass, reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya svāhā. ... [perform the *homa*].

Udvāsanaṃ: Without allowing the wick to burn down to the wick-holder (*śāṇī*), having combined it with the central *brahman* portion, place the *darbha* grass into the clarified butter. There... having pressed both ends with these [implements], facing the flame of the fire, discharge [the offering] through the *astra* mantra into the nostrils, ending with *svāhā*. ... [The act of] *udvāsanaṃ* is performed by means of the *tattva*; [discharge] into the mouth, ending with *svāhā*, by means of the *hṛdaya* mantra. This is *saṃplavanaṃ*.

Having severed the tip of that *darbha*, sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, and cast it into the fire, one should take another *darbha*, consecrate it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, dip its tip into the fire, and place it into the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *astra-mantra*; this is the *pavitrīkaraṇa*.

Having placed that *darbha* blade into the fire with the *astra-mantra*, take another *darbha* blade and, having dipped it in clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *kavaca-mantra*, place it into the fire—this is the *nīrāñjana*. Take yet another *darbha* blade and, having dipped it in the clarified butter with the *astra-mantra*, place it into the fire—this is the *dīpana*. Having untied the *brahmagranthi* at the center of the *śaṇṇī* blades without piercing the tips, place the *darbha* into the clarified butter with the *praṇava*; in this clarified butter...

Having established that the right side and the middle constitute the *pūrvapakṣa* (the first half of the month), *piṅgalā* is the intermediate *kalā*, and the center is *suṣumnā*—[having done so]—one should pour ghee into the right eye of the fire with the *sruc* ladle, saying "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā. Then, having poured ghee into the left eye of the fire with the *sruc* ladle, saying "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā," and then having poured [ghee] into the middle [eye] of the fire, saying "Oṃ hāṃ agni..."

Saying "To Soma and [Agni], Svāhā," he offers into the center of the fire; saying "Oṃ Hāṃ, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā," he offers into one part of the fire; and saying "Svāhā," he pours that clarified butter into the *pātrasthamāna* clarified butter—dividing it into the right, the middle, and the left—saying "Svāhā. This is for the latter fortnight (*apara-pakṣa*). ...ta... (Note: The ellipsis indicates the text continues beyond the provided fragment.)

Having poured ghee on the right side, in the middle, and [on the left], [he offers] with: "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā," "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā," and "Oṃ hāṃ somāgnibhyāṃ... and "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā. Then, into the eye of Agni—namely, the right eye, the middle eye, and the mouth—as well as in front... [he offers] the oblation.

Thereafter, having worshipped the *saṃhitā* alone (the mantra), he shall pour this clarified butter into the clarified butter that has been purified by the heart [mantra]. (p. 17a, l. 1) ... Oṃ hāṃ satyājātāya svāhā; oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā; oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā; oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā— (l. 2) ...

Saying "Svāhā" for each [face], perform the rite of the faces (*vaktrādhi-kāra*): Oṃ haṃ hiṃ satyavāmādevābhyāṃ svāhā | Oṃ hiṃ huṃ vāmā... svāhā | Oṃ huṃ heṃ aghoratatpuruṣābhyāṃ svāhā | Oṃ heṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣeśānābhyāṃ svāhā || Perform the oblation (*homa*) with these mantras, and thus complete the rite of the faces.

"Hem hom satyājātavāmadevāghora-tatpuruṣeśānābhyāṃ svāhā. Having thus performed the kindling of the tongue (*jihvādīpana*), he proceeds as follows: Oṃ am hiraṇyāya svāhā | Oṃ lūm kanakāya svāhā | Oṃ vūm raktāya svāhā | Oṃ śūm kṛṣṇāya svāhā | Oṃ ṣūm suprabhāya svāhā | Oṃ ...

Having performed the *homa* with "Atiraktāya svāhā," "Oṃ hūṃ bahurābhyāṃ svāhā," and so forth, one should perform the visualization of the tongues (*jihvā-nusandhāna*) as follows: "Oṃ śūṃ lūṃ hiraṇyakana-kābhyāṃ svāhā" (l. 7)... "Oṃ lūṃ vūṃ kanakaraktābhyāṃ svāhā. "Oṃ vūṃ śūṃ raktakṛṣṇābhyāṃ svāhā. "Oṃ śūṃ ṣūṃ kṛṣṇasuprabhābhyāṃ svāhā. "Oṃ ṣūṃ sūṃ suprabadhiraktābhyāṃ svāhā. (l. 8).

Having performed the oblation with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ adhiraktabahurūpābhyāṃ svāhā*, one should then perform the visualization of the tongue (*jihvānusandhāna*) and subsequently the unification of the tongues (*jihvaikīkaraṇa*). One who performs the oblation with the mantra *oṃ lūṃ yūṃ vūṃ śūṃ ṣūṃ sūṃ hūṃ hiraṇyakanakaraktakṛṣṇasuprabhātiratnabahurūpābhyāṃ svāhā*—this is the unification of the tongues (*jihvaikīkaraṇa*). Following this, [one performs] the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*).

Taking clarified butter from the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa) up to the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa), perform the *homa*. Afterwards, for the sake of the naming ceremony (*nāmaka-raṇa*), offer three oblations (*āhutitraya*) with [the mantra] "Oṃ hāṃ, you are the fire of Śiva, the consumer of offerings. Having performed the naming, uttering the *hṛdaya* mantra of Vagīśvarākāra, and having raised [the ladle], visualize the face of the Īśāna-mouth of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the *Satyajāta* mantra, and [offer] the six substances beginning with gold through the central mouth.

Having joined—(l.4) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and culminating in *vaṣaṭ*, one who is about to offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) should take the *sruk* and fill it; then, upon it—(l.5)...

Placing the face [of the ladle] downward and setting a flower upon its tip, having firmly grasped the *śaṅkhākāra* (conch-shaped handle) with the right hand in front and the left hand behind—[he who is] endowed with the *sruva* and the *sruc* which were brought forth from the *ye... (ṛju-sthita)*, and who possesses eyes placed upon the tip of the *sruc* held at the navel; having placed the base of the *sruc* within the *yidamūla* (the root of the support), without wavering, by means of a thread of the measure of a *ner* (leaf)... *(Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a ritual manual (*paddhati*) describing the preparation of sacrificial implements. The bracketed portions indicate conjectural reconstructions based on the context of Vedic/Tantric ritual procedures.)*

Having uttered the root mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ*, one shall perform the homa of all the *ātmanas* into the fire. This is the *pūrṇāhuti*. After this, having taken up the various parts of the fire for the sake of the *caru*, and having preserved them in another location, one shall subsequently perform the homa of sixteen palāśa fuel-sticks—measuring fourteen fingers in length—into the fire by means of the vowels beginning with ‘A’.
Then: "Seated upon a white lotus throne, five-faced and four-armed..."
With a long beard, he was the embodiment of Brahman, his head adorned with a crown of matted locks.
With circles of froth on his cheeks, eyes like staffs, and hands busy with a garland— having meditated thus,
he [is visualized] within the heart-lotus as red-complexioned, three-eyed, and endowed with hands holding the weapons of Śiva.

Having meditated in this manner, one should address Agni with the words: "O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, the supreme purifier... therefore, having established Śiva within the lotus of your heart, one should worship Him. Having thus petitioned Agni, one should then enter through the middle channel of Agni’s body... having worshipped [Śiva] within your own heart-lotus as before, beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and accompanied by His attendants, and having offered incense and lamps, [one should contemplate] the mouth of Śiva... Agni...

Having performed meditation and emerged [from the heart], one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Visualize that it emerges from the nose and tongue of Śiva residing in the *agni-sthāna* (the fire-center), and—(l.

6)—having gone without interruption like a ray of light through the *śikhā-nāḍī* (the crest-channel) of Yāgeśvara, it dissolves and remains attached even in the *irani* (fire-pit) location; thus meditate... (l. 7)... Having established the connection of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*) for Śiva in the *kumbha-sthāna* (the water-pot center), for Śiva as Yāgeśvara, and for Śiva in the *agni-sthāna*, thereafter, for the purpose of offering general and specific *darbha* grasses... (l. 8)...

... having performed the *homa*, and having performed the *daśāṃśa-homa* for the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*), he should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Thereafter, for the sake of pacifying ill omens, for an auspicious place and time, and as a cause for [the disciple’s] birth, he shall perform one hundred oblations with the Root Mantra (*mūla*). For the purpose of the disciple’s entry (*śiṣyapraveśana*), he shall perform the *homa* for each individual disciple separately one hundred times with the Root Mantra, accompanied by the *pūrṇāhuti*. He shall then perform the *darpaṇa* and *dīpana* for the mantras beginning with Śiva.

Performing [the rite] as follows: Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā—oṃ hom īśānamūrtaye svāhā; oṃ hem tatpuruṣavaktrāya svāhā; oṃ him aghorahṛdayāya svāhā; oṃ him vāmadevaguhyāya svāhā; oṃ ham sadyojāta-mūrtaye svāhā; oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā; oṃ hīm śirase svāhā; oṃ hūm śikhāyai svāhā; oṃ haiṃ kavacāya svāhā; oṃ hahā netrebhyaḥ svāhā; oṃ haḥ.

Offer one oblation for each with "Astrāya Svāhā. Then perform the *darpaṇa* (mirror-offering): Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hūṃ śivāya huṃ phaṭ. Oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ īśānāya huṃ phaṭ. Oṃ hūṃ heṃ hūṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya huṃ phaṭ. Oṃ hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ aghorahṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ. Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ hūṃ vāmadevaguhyāya [huṃ phaṭ]. Oṃ hūṃ haṃ hūṃ sadyojātamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ. Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ haṃ hiṃ huṃ śirase huṃ phaṭ; oṃ hūṃ haṃ hūṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ; oṃ hūṃ haiṃ hūṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ; oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hūṃ netrebhyo huṃ phaṭ; oṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ.

Having performed the homa three times for each of these mantras—namely the dīpana—and thereafter, in accordance with the procedure for sthālīpāka, [one should take] a vessel that is free from defects such as being made of copper, earthenware, or having a broken rim.

Having suspended [the thread] with the *kavaca* [mantra], performed the *avaguṇṭhana* [concealment] with the same, and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa*, worshipped it with the *candana* and other offerings, offered incense (*dhūpa*), and having consecrated it with both the *kavaca* and the *astra* mantras, one should sprinkle with the *astra* the pavilion that has been encircled by three blades of *darbha* grass and smeared with cow dung, and perform the *avaguṇṭhana* with the *kavaca*. With the *astra*... [text continues].

Having spread darbha grass and worshipped the Ṣaḍutthāsana upon it, and having placed this vessel upon it, one should worship Śiva therein until midnight. Then, taking those flowers and placing them [in the vessel], one should smear it with clarified butter from a cow consecrated by the Astra-mantra, strain it through a cloth, and perform the purificatory rites beginning with Nīrīkṣaṇa. Then, having milked the cow’s milk consecrated in nine ways by the Mūla-mantra, [one should prepare] the rice-gruel (*yāntrika-tandulodana*)...

Having placed five small stones for one disciple and one *śiraṅkāya* for each subsequent disciple (l. 5), [he places them] to the south, east, and west of the *kuṇḍa*. Having positioned the supporting base facing east, he rubs it with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkles it (*prokṣita*), performs the enclosure (*avaguṇṭhana*) with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having cast the previously prepared *śivāgni* [into it], he places the sacrificial ladle (*caru-sthālī*) upon it.

Having covered the vessel with a lid and so forth using the Astra-mantra, having performed the encasement (avaguṇṭhana) with the Kavaca-mantra, and having caused the fire to blaze with the Astra-mantra, he shall cook it thoroughly and evenly by means of the Hrasva-prāsāda-mantra.

If it has been slow to burn, or if various diseases have arisen, one should consider that there is a foul odor. For the sake of its pacification, one should perform a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra, joined with the Svāhā-ending mantras. Having performed the *taptābhikāra* (heating) with "Oṃ susvanyo bhava" and having sprinkled the pavilion with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍuttāsana*) as before, place [the vessel] upon it, and conclude with the Vauṣaṭ-ending [mantra].

With the *saṃhitā-mantras*, beginning with "śītalo bhava," [he performs] the cooling rite (*śītābhikāra*). Thereafter, having smeared the outer surface of the *caru*-vessel with clay and having drawn a mandala to the east of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he worships the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) therein, places [the vessel] upon it, worships it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and performs an oblation (*homa*) into the fire with the *saṃhitā-mantras* ending in "svāhā. Then, saying "svāhā," he pours a stream of abundant clarified butter over the *caru* using the *sruva* ladle.

After this *sambhāra-homa*, having consecrated [the offering] with the Saṃhitā mantras ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having offered it with the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should inform the Lord of the Maṇḍala, saying, "This is the portion. Then, dividing that *caru* into three parts, one offers a generous amount of ghee and honey from one part to the Lord of the Maṇḍala, the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *kumbhastha*, and the *śivāgni*, and after presenting it, one offers incense, lamps, and so forth.

Having performed the *upāntama* (or *mukhāntama*) worship... [he], together with his disciple, having set aside abundant ghee and honey for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), performed one hundred and eight *homa* offerings and the final *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, for the disciple, he performed the removal of impurity (*vimatāpana*). "O Blessed One, I have been instructed; you, as the authorized one, must show favor to these disciples. [mā...]

Now, those who have approached with devotion according to the characteristics described above—[meaning] these disciples who, having been initiated by Your Lordship while You were acting as the presiding authority (*adhiṣṭhāna*), have now [been]... initiated; and these disciples, being graced by Your Lordship, possess the characteristics spoken of in the *śāstra* regarding me...

Having petitioned, "O Lord, please grant me permission so that I may become fit for meditating upon Your venerable lotus feet," and having received that permission, [the preceptor] bathed and observed a fast. Then, having summoned the disciple who remained fasting, he led him out from the interior of the maṇḍapa to the north of the western door, drew a maṇḍala there, and [placed] the eastern... within it.

Having placed flower-akṣatas and performed the meditation upon the Praṇava within them, he should summon the disciple from the *añjali-hasta* position; having restrained him so that he faces north therein, [the preceptor], standing on his right side... with divine vision, while reciting the *mūla-mantra*, should wash [him].

Having sprinkled [him] with the Astra-mantra for the purpose of bathing, he should strike him on the head with ashes for the sake of an ash-bath while reciting the Astra-mantra; then, having again sprinkled his head with the Astra-mantra, he should touch him above the navel with the tips of Darbha grass for the purpose of purification (*mārjana*), and below the navel with the roots of the Darbha grass in the reverse order; then, with the Astra-mantra, [he should touch] his heart-region.

For the sake of bestowing all excellent qualities, one should touch him and meditate upon his Self; then, having performed the nyāsa of the *mūrdhamaṃtra* in the heart and the *saṃhitāmantras* in their respective locations within his body, one should apply a tilaka with sandalwood paste, worship Śiva upon his head, place flowers in his hand, sprinkle him with the *astra-mantra*, perform the *avaguṇṭhana* with the *kavaca-mantra*, and [employ] the *mūlamaṃtra*... (p. 20b).

Having bound his eyes with a consecrated new cloth using the Netra-mantra, and having held his hands, he leads him clockwise around the pavilion. Having stationed him in the presence of Śiva, he performs the Netra-bandhana, offers a handful of flowers, and bows to Śiva. Thereafter, having prepared a maṇḍala to the right of Śiva, he prepares the seat of Praṇava within it for Śiva.

Facing himself, he should discharge the Astra-mantra into the heart of the disciple and strike him with flowers. Then, having received his soul (*ātman*) by means of the Saṃhāramudrā with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," he should lead it to and place it within the disciple's *dvādaśānta*. [He should then dissolve] the disciple's elemental body (*bhūtadeha*) through the Nivṛtti-kalā and the others...

Having performed purification preceded by *pūraka* [breathing], one should perform the immersion (*āplāvana*) of the form of the Supreme Space (*paramākāśarūpa*) into the station of Śakti. Then, having uttered the primordial mantra (*ādyamantra*) upon the pericarp of his heart-lotus, one should draw back and establish the Self residing within the twelve thousand [channels] (*dvādaśāntastha-nāḍī*). Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) beginning with the seat-form (*āsanamūrti*), one should touch him from the head downwards with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), perform the binding of the eyes (*netrabandhana*), fashion the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*), and meditate upon him as being of the nature of radiant light (*tejo-rūpa*).

Having recited the *prāsāda* mantra (l. 8), and having gone with the disciple who has received the twelve-fold peaceful recitation (*anuṣṭhāna*), he places it upon the disciple’s head for the purpose of warding off obstacles; then, having whispered the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) into the right ear (l. 9)... [having received] the word, thereafter, having caused the *muṇḍahasta* and *kumbhastha* to offer salutations with handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and having brought them to the corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [he places them] on his right side in the mandala (p. 21a, l. 1)...

Having visualized the sacrificial seat (*vāsana*), one who establishes the disciple within it as the fire should place the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass upon his own knee and foot, and then... (l. 2) ... [proceeds].

Having placed [the breath] through the root-mantra into the disciple's body, one should contemplate that the disciple’s central channel (*nāḍī*), which is like a lotus fiber, originates from his *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] and enters his own heart through the middle [of the disciple's body] by means of the *pūraka* breath; having thus dissolved it by means of the *kumbhaka*, one should then contemplate that [one's own breath], originating from one's own *reca* breath, emerges through the disciple's *piṅgalā* and enters the disciple's heart by means of the *pūraka*.

In this manner, having remained within oneself, it may dissolve into Śiva at the *kumbhasthāna*; having emerged from Śiva at the *kumbhasthāna*, it may dissolve into Sthandileśvara; having remained within Sthandileśvara, it may emerge and dissolve into Śiva at the *vahnisthāna*. Having thus established the continuity of the *nāḍī*, this is the *sthitamātṛkā*. Then, perform the threefold *ārati* by means of the root mantra (*āmūla*). After that—

Having performed the *sampātahoma* upon the head of the disciple with the *saṃhitā-mantra*, and having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) for the sake of the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahastasthārtha*), and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should thereafter establish himself according to the tradition, instruct him in the *saṃhitā-mantras*, prostrate to Śiva, and prostrate to himself as well. In this manner, by means of the initiation into the *samaya*, the disciple becomes fit for the service of the Guru.

Having completed the sacrifice by means of this initiation alone (*samayadīkṣā*), one should worship Agnisthāna Śiva with the root mantra (*mūla*). Then, taking sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the purpose of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra. Having performed the worship beginning with the sipping of water (*ācamana*) as a preliminary, and having offered the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpa*), one should worship the flower. Then, according to the method prescribed for the special consecration (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*), one should perform the oblation (*bali*) for Brahmā and the others, as well as for Indra and the others, including the inner oblation (*antarbali*) and the outer oblation (*bahirbali*).

Having performed [the rites], he shall conclude the sacrifice. Otherwise, one must perform the *viśeṣasaṃskāra* immediately; without offering the *naivedya* and other items to Śiva in the four fire-locations (*agnisthāna*), one performs the *viśeṣasaṃskāra*.
Then, by the power of Śiva’s hand, he shall go to the world of Śiva (*śivaloka*).
The procedure for the *samayadīkṣā* is completed. Salutations to the venerable Gurus who are identical with Śiva.
Nivṛtti is proclaimed to have the luster of molten gold, to be adorned by the moon-like four faces, and to hold a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, and a garland.
Resembling pure crystal, she has two faces and four arms;
holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is adorned with jewels of the [stage of] Pratiṣṭhā.

Red in color, with matted hair and a crescent moon, she has three faces and four arms; holding a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she resembles the blazing fire of knowledge.
(Verse 7) She has four faces, four arms, is black in color, and possesses great power.
She holds a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; he wears a sacred thread and has a serpent as his emblem for the sake of peace.
Resembling pure crystal, she has five faces and four arms;
holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a water-lily, she bestows the boons of Peace, Beyond-Peace, and Supreme Grace.
O child, she who dwells upon the chest of Keśava and upon the lotus of Śambhu as Umā—
On the left side, O lotus-seated one, O moon-faced one, Vāṇī and Bhaṃ are in the royal [posture].
As long as the sun remains in the sky, so long shall the fortune of your lineage, together with sons and grandsons, endure firmly upon its established footing.

Thereafter, having requested the *saṃskāradīkṣā*... [he] should perform the *saṃskāradīkṣā*. Having worshipped them with meditation (*dhyāna*) preceded by the recitation of "Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ" and "Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ" within the heart-lotus of Śivāgnis, and having performed their invocation (*āvāhana*), he should subsequently offer barley-oblations (*yavāhuti*) individually with the Heart-mantra for the sake of their presence (*sannidhāna*). Then, having sprinkled the disciple's heart with the Astra-mantra, [he recites] "Oṃ haḥ."

Having performed the *tāḍana* with flowers while reciting *hūṃ phaṭ*, one enters his heart through one's own *rāśaka* while reciting *oṃ hūṃ*. Having meditated upon his consciousness as shining like the constellation Śravaṇa, one should offer salutation to oneself with: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*.

Having brought [the soul] by means of the *dvādaśānta* of that [deity], one should meditate upon the Self in the form of the Bindu at the tip of the qualities (*guṇāgra-bindurūpa*), utter the *ātma-mantra*, and taking it up with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, cause it to enter one’s own heart by means of one’s own *pūraka* breath. Then, through *kumbhaka*, having unified oneself and that [soul], and having contemplated the *mūla-mantra*, one should utter the *ātma-mantra* by means of *recaka* in the sequence of abandoning the causes beginning with Brahmā.

Having taken [the substance] up to its own limit of twelve *āntas* and joined it at the *śivanidhi*, and again (l. 8), having brought it back up to the limit of the *brūmadhya* according to the order of emanation (*sr̥ṣṭikrama*), one should meditate upon oneself as the one who bestows the divine gift (*devatādāna*) into the *vāgīśvarī-garbhanāḍī* by taking [it] through the southern channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) and using the *utpavamudrā*. (l. 9) Having uttered the *ātma-mantra* and performed one hundred oblations (*homa*) with the root mantra for the sake of the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*) beginning with the *garbhadāna*, one should perform [the rite] in front of the disciple.

One who purifies committed sins by means of the characteristics of fire— [even] one who has violated the Guru’s bed becomes purified through the Pavitra, scents, and the recitation of the Bhūḥ-mantra.
*pavitrā gandhaiḥ sa bhūhartābhyanaṅgān gurutalpagah* |
The drinker of liquor, the slayer of a guru, the killer of a cow, and the destroyer of what has been done;
[he who is] a consumer of the fetus and the destroyer of the womb, while Kṛṣṇa and Agni are present in the mouth of the corpse.
In the fire of a black [substance], and in the smell of a corpse, there is the destruction of the fetus and the husband;
when the fire flickers like a woman,
it trembles in the hands of a goldsmith.

When the fetus is killed, the embryo-destroyer’s latent impurity (*niṣṭejaḥ*) bursts forth within the child. Thus, having understood [this] through the fire (*vahni*), in order to destroy those sins, one should perform [the rite] with the *Aghora* mantra: *oṃ haṃ sākṣamalarayūṃ sakalavyāpta... śivāya namaḥ*. By means of this *Navātman* mantra, having understood the increase and decrease of the sins through the signs of the fire, the performer of the *homa* should first [offer oblations].

Thereafter, for the purification of the womb-seed (*yoni-bīja*), food, sins, and the [nine] planets, he should inform Śiva, saying "O Dvija-Nāgaveṇu," offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra, and request that [the recipient] become a portion of Rudra; then, offering three oblations with the root mantra and consecrating it with the root mantra, he should give the sacred thread (*upavīta*). For a Brāhmaṇa, it should end with "Śivāntam"; for a Kṣatriya, it should end with "Devāntam"; for a Vaiśya, it should end with "Īśvarāntam"; and for a Śūdra...

Having performed the naming ceremony for the Śūdra ending with *devānta* (l. 8), for the women ending with *śakti*, and for the others ending with *gaṇa*, one who performs one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) with the root mantra, followed by a ten-part oblation (*daśāṃśa-homa*) for the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*), and then offers the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Thereafter, having extracted the soul—which remains possessing the light of the Jvālāgra-samāna fire—by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* from the fire, one brings it with the *pūraka* breath into one’s own heart-lotus. Then, by means of the *kumbhaka* breath, having effected its unification with Śiva within the heart-lotus, one recites the root mantra and, by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* along with the *recaka* breath, [dissolves it] through the sequence of abandoning the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, up to the end of the twelve [levels] into Śiva.

Having joined [the mantras] again and returned through the stages of creation as far as the *bindu-sthāna*, one should carry the disciple into his filled body (*pūrṇadeha*) by means of the *utpatti-mudrā* while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ. Having placed him there, one should sprinkle his head with the water of the *arghya*. Then, having awakened Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, one should perform the homa with the root mantra for the emergence of the fire and the emergence of the food, as a cause for atonement (*prāyaścitta*), and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having worshipped Śiva with his disciple, having made him prostrate before himself, and having bestowed blessings upon him, he shall instruct him in the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), saying to him: "You are eligible for the worship of the Śivāgnikuṇḍa, for the hearing of the scriptures (*śāstraśravaṇa*), and for the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*). Thereafter, taking Śivāgni, the Śivakuṇḍa, Maṇḍaleśvara, and others as witnesses, he shall teach the rules of conduct:
"One should not revile the Cause, the God, nor the scripture spoken by Him; one should not revile the Guru, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the Śaiva, or the Liṅga."

In the case of a *nādya-liṅga*, there is no *nirmālya* (remnant of offerings), nor are there [ordinary] substances; one initiated by Śiva must perform the worship of Śiva’s fire and the Guru according to the prescribed rule.
He who would thus establish the *samayas* (initiates) or purify children and others—[he is the true practitioner].

To those such as children and others who have not received initiation (*akṛtākāra*), he shall first perform one hundred and eight oblations with the *mūla-mantra* as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Having thus purified them through the conduct of the observance (*samayācāraśuddhi*), he shall then instruct them in the *kūṭinamantra*.

Thereafter, for the various people desiring to enter the Śivāśrama, having placed the staff (*daṇḍa*), the kaupīna, the sacred ash (*bhasma*), the girdle (*upavīta*), the matted hair (*jaṭā*), the ochre robe (*kāṣāya*), and the crest-jewel (*śikhāmaṇi*) individually in separate vessels, and having purified them by means of inspection and other rites, he should consecrate them with the five Brahmans or with the [mantras] beginning with the Heart; then, having performed the *saṃpātahoma*, he should offer them from the vicinity of the water-pot (*kumbha*), bow down, and [bestow them] upon the living beings.

The preceptor shall grant the disciple the Śivāgni and the Śivakuṇḍa with [these] as witnesses; he (the disciple), in turn, shall accept them, saying, "I take [them], with the Śivāgni and the others as my witnesses."

Thereafter, having worshipped Śiva, who resides in the fire, with the root mantra, one should take sacrificial rice (*caru*) for the purpose of the food offering (*naivedya*), perform three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra, and offer water for sipping (*ācamanārghya*). Having presented sandalwood paste, betel leaves, and other purifying items (*pavitraka*), one should reduce [the offering] to ashes, offer water for sipping again, and perform *japa*. Then, having offered the food, scattered the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpa*), and prostrated, one should offer water for sipping to the one facing away (*parāṅmukha*), fashion the *mūrti*, and [dismiss] Śiva, who resides in the fire.

Having performed the *utthāpana* (raising), and subsequently having performed the *homa* with the *pūrādimantras*, one should unite the mantras for the stationing of the fire (*agnisthānana-mantras*) within one’s own heart. Having paid obeisance to the Fire and worshipped it with "Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ śivāya namaḥ," one should raise and awaken the Fire. Then, having offered oblations (*bali*) to Brahmā and the others who occupy the sacrificial ground (*paridhiviṣṭara-sthāna*), as well as to Indra and the other guardians of the quarters, and having given the water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the arghya...

Having offered the *parāṅmukhārghya* and performed the *utthāpana* of Brahmā and the others, as well as Indra and the rest, he places a *yīraṇa* mandala to his right at the corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Within that mandala, for the purpose of the intermediate offerings (*antarbali*), he offers in the directions—east, south, west, and north—the following: *Oṃ hāṃ rudrebhyo namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ mātṛbhyo namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ gaṇebhyo namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ yakṣebhyo namaḥ*.

Having worshipped thus, one should also worship in these intermediate directions—Īśāna, Agni, Nirṛti, and Vāyu—with: *Oṃ hāṃ grahebhyaḥ namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ asurebhyaḥ namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ rākṣasebhyaḥ namaḥ*, and *Oṃ hāṃ nāgebhyaḥ namaḥ*. Then, in the center of that maṇḍala, in the Īśāna, Agni, and Nirṛti corners, one should worship with: *Oṃ hāṃ nakṣatrebhyaḥ namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ rāśibhyaḥ namaḥ*, and *Oṃ hāṃ viśvebhyaḥ namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ kṣetrapālakāya namaḥ" between Vāyu and Varuṇa, and having offered arghya, one should perform the external bali-offering in the eight directions starting from the east within the second maṇḍala to Indra and the other guardians of the quarters, Brahmā in the northeast, and Viṣṇu in the northwest; and in the center, [worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ nīlalohitāya namaḥ."

Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya*, he shall offer the *antarbali* and *bahirbali* ending with *svāhā* for the Rudras and others first, and for Indra and others afterwards; then, having performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), he shall otherwise [recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ! Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds, those dwelling in fierce abodes, and whoever there may be who dwell in gentle abodes."

May Mātṛkā, who is of the form of Rudra, and those who are the leaders of the Gaṇas, as well as others who have arrived from the various quarters and intermediate directions—all with minds full of great joy—accept this offering; may they quickly protect us from all calamities. With this mantra, one should perform the offering accompanied by the *kūṭa*.

Thereafter, having given the *parāṅmukhārghya* to these [deities] and having caused them to depart (*udvāpita*), he should unite them within his own heart. Then, having performed *ācamana* and *nyāsa*, he should worship Śiva located in the maṇḍala with the eight flowers, offer salutations, give the *parāṅmukhārghya*, perform the *mūrdhi* [rite], and unite Śiva located in the pot (*kumbha*). Having worshipped Śiva located in the pot with the eight flowers—

Having prostrated and offered the *parāṅmukhārghya*, he should perform the *mūrtipratiṣṭhā*. Having worshipped the *astravartanī* and performed the *mūrtipratiṣṭhā*, he should unite Śiva, who resides within the *kumbha-sthāna*, with the *astravartanī* and join them within his own heart. Having prostrated, he should offer the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpa*), perform the *ṣaḍdhā*, the hymn of praise (*stotra*), circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), and prostration. Then, having offered the *parāṅmukhārghya* and performed the *mūrtipratiṣṭhā*, he should make this petition: "May you please forgive all my transgressions."

Having offered the *arghya* with its face turned away from the sacrificial deities (*parāṅmukhārghya*) and having performed their dismissal (*udvāsana*), he should thereafter worship Caṇḍeśvara in the mandala shaped like the half-moon according to the eternal procedure, as if he were Śiva himself, and then fashion his [Caṇḍeśvara’s] form. Subsequently, taking up the mantras residing in the *arghyapātra*, he shall unite them within his own heart; thus the special consecration (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*) is completed. [He then proceeds to] the world of Śrīkaṇṭha...

Having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) through the specific refinements (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*) by the power of Śivahasta, after one year has passed, the Guru, for the sake of the disciple who is fit for liberation, performs the *nirvāṇadīkṣā*—excluding the removal of the disciple’s impurity (*malabhāga*) and the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*). In the performance of the *nirvāṇadīkṣā*, as before, there is the worship of the lords of the gates (*dvāradvāreśvarapūjā*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antarayāga*), and the three *arghya*s...

Having performed the *kuṇḍa-saṃskāra* (purification of the fire-pit), the *maṇḍapa-pūjā* (worship of the pavilion), and all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) for the sacred fire beginning with *nāmakaraṇa* up to its establishment (*agnisthāpana*), as well as the special purificatory rites (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*) for Śiva’s worship—including *darpaṇa*, *dīpana*, and *sthālīpāka*—and having performed the *prāyaścitta-homa* (expiatory oblation), one should perform the *darpaṇa* and *dīpana* for the mantras beginning with the *mūla-mantra* and ending with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of the *nirvāṇadīkṣā* (liberating initiation), just as before; thereafter, one should worship Śiva with the *mūla-mantra*.
Having paid homage to Śiva,

he shall address a petition to the Lord Śiva: "He who has been tested, who is capable, and who has approached for the sake of liberation— [him I address] with my vital breaths moving within and without."
One of noble birth, established in the times of the portions of Īśa—
therefore, let this palace be constructed for the sake of liberation within this very place.

Having made this request, saying, "May it be so, as permitted by the Supreme Lord," and having performed the visualization (*bhāvanā*), one should subsequently draw a maṇḍala to the south of the Śivāgni. Having prepared the seat of the Praṇava (*praṇavāsana*) therein, one should station the disciple within it. Then, performing the purification of his elemental body (*bhūtadeha-śuddhi*) according to the prescribed method, one should perform the ablution (*āplāvana*). Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Kalās, beginning with Śāntyatītā and the rest, upon the five locations of the Kalās, starting from the Brahma-randhra down to the feet.

Having performed the nyāsa of the heart-mantras and other mantras in the locations such as the heart, and having offered the mahāmudrā and worshipped with the root mantra, one should then take a thread wound around the forefinger three times, fold it into three, sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra, perform the avaguṇṭhana with the Kavaca-mantra, worship and consecrate it with the root mantra, and place it above upon the twelve-finger-high crest [of the linga] at Śiva’s primary location.

Leaving aside the four-finger-width thread (*catur-aṅgula-sūtra*), one should bind [the cord] with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) from the big toe to the end of the foot like a palm-tree trunk. For a male, it should be joined on the right side of the *suṣumnā*, and for a female, on the left side. Having performed the *satyādhi-vāsa* (dwelling of truth), if one wishes to conclude the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should perform the purification (*saṃskāra*) as before for the *pāśa-sūtra*, and likewise purify the ritual action (*kriyā*) through the purifications such as *nirīkṣaṇa*.
